Then call old school Trek fans the original sci fi hipsters, there were plenty of us who liked it before it was "cool." edit:  To elaborate in a more serious tone, Trek may not have had blockbuster wins at the box office but to say it wasn't as popular as we believe it was is a complete misconception.  Think about the impact Trek has had on society and you'll see how wrong that is. The first space shuttle hot its name because of the show.  There's probably not a person walking this earth that wouldn't recognize the Enterprise if you showed it to them.  (The starship, that is.)  Terminology and phrases from the show have entered the cultural lexicon.  Generations of scientists, engineers, doctors and people from all walks of life were inspired by the series.  A ridiculous amount of the technology in today's world was inspired directly by Trek.  We only haver some of the tech we have *because* of Trek.  To say it wasn't popular just isn't true. Now as to why it wasn't more commercially or broadly successful, that's another issue.  I really think that's a cultural/societal thing.  It really wasn't "ok" or "acceptable" to be a sci fi geek until the last fifteen years or so.  The pre-internet days made it a lot harder to find a group of people who thought the way you did and enjoyed what you did.  When I was a kid nobody would admit to liking Star Trek or reading comics.  You were ostracized and shunned and sometimes at risk when you did admit to being a geek.  I went to see a major Trek movie in the theater opening week, first Trek I'd ever gotten seen in the theater, and when I was buying the ticket, saying "One for Star Trek" someone stuck gum in my hair and in the theater I got a soda and popcorn thrown at me.       Now, with people of my generation getting to be in control of things like movies and TV and the internet being able to make fans come together easier and even exposing the genre to people who wouldn't have thought they'd be fans, it's broadened the popularity, made it more palatable, more acceptable.  I don't think anyone has a problem admitting they read comics or like Star Trek now.  It's ok.  You can wait for hours in line outside a theater wearing your Starfleet uniform and it's all right, it's ok, people are going to high five you and be right there with you.  20, 30 years ago?  Not a chance.  Today, it's not just all right, it's sort of expected.  And that's good for all of us. Like someone else said, The Martian was a big hit.  There's no shortage of thinking-man's sci-fi out there.  Trek was founded on that idea and now that society at large isn't as biased or judgemental against it, there's no reason we shouldn't have it.  Trek was always popular.  It just wasn't always ok for all of us out here to show it.

Hey there, someone here to answer your questions about mobile home living. First and most important thing to keep in mind is that mobile or manufactured homes depreciate in value, unlike condos or traditional homes which appreciate.  Traditional home will sell for say, a significant amount and five years later you can sell it for more. Mobile homes work the opposite way.  Say you got for a moderate amount and it was a resale, four years old. Brand new, it sold for more.  If and when you sell this home, you can expect to probably break even.  You won't necessarily get your investment back. However, you don't put that much into it. Tradeoff. Compared to renting, it's really not a bad investment. When you consider rent will go up, your mortgage never will (space rent might, however--more on that in a moment), factor in first, last, security deposit, rising rent, you're almost even with what it would cost to purchase a mobile home and you're not sharing walls or upstairs/downstairs situations with neighbors.  As for the rent I mentioned--except in some rare cases, you own the home but not the land it sits on. The park or community you're in owns the land. In theory you could have the home moved elsewhere if you really wanted to. The parks charge a monthly rent for the space your home sits on. That amount varies greatly depending on the park, the place within the park and the size of the space. Just like an apartment, they have the right to raise that rent every year, how much and if they will depends on varying factors, mostly their community rules. When you take the space rent and mortgage together, it's maybe a bit more than apartment rent in some places, less than in others, and almost always less than the mortgage of a traditional home. Those parks or communities, think of them like an HOA. They have rules and bylaws, things you can and can't do, most are fairly lenient but sometimes there are restrictions on pets, dogs and their sizes, how many you can have, certainly that you shouldn't leave them unleashed to wander the neighborhood, where you can park your car(s), things of that nature. They may be on you occasionally about upkeep and maintenance on your yard and home. If it needs painting, some external cosmetic work, weed the yard, etc, etc. Some find this restrictive and don't want to deal with it. Me, having lived in a neighborhood where people didn't care and there was a hoarder house across the street, I'm glad they keep on these things.  For what it's worth, some of those parks/communities are extremely nice.  Security, clubhouses, gyms.  The more amenities the higher the space rent but it's a get what you pay for situation.   Repairs and maintenance on the house is your responsibility. If there's a problem with the electrical or plumbing outside the house on park property, it's usually the park management's responsibility to fix it.  As for the homes themselves, it depends largely on the manufacturer and age but most of them now are extremely well built, to the point that if you were blindfolded and taken inside, you probably couldn't tell the difference between a mobile or "manufactured" home and a traditional home. In some cases, it's arguable better than traditional home since they're newer and built with the most modern supplies.  Your homeowner's insurance may be a little bit higher than a traditional home. This depends on where the home is. Many of the mobile home parks are situated in the foothills or in "fire zones" so that raises it a bit. Nothing obscene but if you've ever had a traditional homeowner's insurance policy you'd notice the difference.  You'll still have property taxes but they're considerably lower than those of a traditional home. All in all, there's absolutely nothing wrong with living in a mobile home in the right community and if it's the right unit. It's a question of finance, really, in the end.  Consider this: That mobile home—you'll pay in the area of a moderate monthly amount for mortgage and space rent for a 3 bed, 2 bath 1400 sq ft 5 year old home with central air and heat in (if you get into the right park or community) a gated community that provides 24/7 security, a pool, gym, tennis and basketball courts and community center. A 1000 sq ft 2 bed 1 bath apt in an unsecured building with a window ac and wall furnace from the 40's in an ok part of town might run you a similar monthly amount. You won't make a profit when you sell the house but you wouldn't when you leave the apt either, would you? That's what it comes down to for most people--long term potential. If you're looking at possible future money from the place, you're not likely to get it. If that's not an issue, then it's not a bad investment in housing.   Feel free to check out:  www.mhvillage.com  It's a listing site for available mobile homes nationwide.  New manufactured/mobile homes sell through dealers.  Resales can go through dealers or your average realtor, depending on the seller's preference.

Unpopular opinion:  A famous villain wasn't redeemed.   The character was never a very good person and kept getting worse. A rival leader decides to take control of the nation in the fading days of the war, murders the partner, goes after the dictator's son and the dictator kills the rival.  The dictator is captured and brought before the court.  When the world is faced with the evidence--countries invades, people tortured, the bodies of millions dead litter the countryside.
